title: When the gods, like man: the labor of the Igigi and the creation of humankind from clay and a slain god's flesh

translation.sourceText: Akkadian reconstruction from named scholarly editions (Lambert & Millard 1969, the critical edition; George & Al-Rawi 1996 for the Old Babylonian Sippar witnesses; Foster 2005 Before the Muses 3rd ed.). Line-numbering follows Lambert–Millard 1969.
translation.sourceLicense: Best-effort reconstruction; scholarly editions cited as references; English original to this project (CC0-1.0).
translation.sourceUrl: (no openly-licensed digital source — see source-akk-1.json citations; eBL L.1.1 consulted as collation aid only, CC BY-NC, not reproduced)
translation.sourceAccessedVia: Best-effort reconstruction (Lambert–Millard 1969 + George & Al-Rawi 1996 + Foster 2005; eBL L.1.1 collation aid)
translation.verificationStatus: best-effort-reconstruction-pending-verification; sign-by-sign transliteration pending collation against Lambert–Millard 1969 and eBL L.1.1
translation.reviewer: approved — all 111 lines + 10 glossary entries defensible; zero lens-leakage; Assyriologically serious (a69daaa6). Reconstruction sign-collation pending.
translation.humanRuling: 2026-07-04: Human-ratified extension of the standing lens-neutral policy. The Elohim/ancient-astronaut anthropogony reading is kept OUT of the translation and glossary (proposed-not-committed speculative entry 'atrahasis-labor-force-anthropogony-elohim-frame'), routed to the Explainer 'made-from-the-ground-to-bear-the-labor'. The I:1 frame-crux ships the Lambert-Millard comparative 'When the gods, like man' (the LESS lens-congenial reading); Foster's identity reading documented-not-adopted. Akkadian remains best-effort — sign-level collation against Lambert-Millard 1969 / eBL L.1.1 pending (reviewer flags I:233 -sha->-shunu, I:191 eli); verificationStatus holds.

reviewerReport.scope: Atra-hasis Tablet I (WoH translation): all 111 reconstructed lines re-parsed independently from the transliterated Akkadian (Lambert & Millard 1969 critical edition) against source-akk-1.json. Anthropogony core: the divine labor-frame, the Igigi rebellion, Enki's lullu proposal, the slaughter of We-ila, and the fourteen clay pieces.
reviewerReport.reviewNote: Independent Akkadian re-parse confirms every rendering and note. Verified against CAD/AHw and named editions: inuma ilu awilum I:1 comparative-vs-identity crux (Lambert-Millard/von Soden vs Foster 2005) correctly stated and the identity reading flagged 'documented, not adopted'; dullu/supsikku thesis-vocabulary (CAD D 173; CAD S/3 326); lullu I:192-199 (CAD L 242 'primitive man', cf. Enuma Elis VI:6); awilum lissi dulli ili I:195 anthropogony thesis-line with the Genesis 1:26 selem/demut labor-vs-image contrast (Clifford 1994, Middleton 2005) in apparatus; the siru/damu/tiddu flesh-blood-clay triad I:212-225 (Kilmer 1972, Moran 1970, Batto 1992) and the Genesis 2:7 divergence (dust+breath, no slain deity, no blood) accurately drawn; etemmu I:217 as the kispu-sustained ancestral ghost (CAD E 397); the We-ila double pun I:222 (we-e ila -> awilu; temu -> etemmu; Moran 1970, Abusch 1998) correctly stated and explicitly disclaiming any engineered-cognition reading; uppu 'drum(?)' I:216 and urutam 'freedom(?)' I:242 cruxes correctly marked uncertain (AHw 1435 birth-stool alternative noted); the seven-and-seven fourteen-pieces (imittu/sumelu/libittu) correct. Lens-leakage: NONE — every English line reads as a defensible scholarly translation; the anthropogony, slain god, and etemmu are rendered plainly with no Elohim/ancient-astronaut intrusion (the speculative frame is routed OUT to the Explainer per the 2026-07-04 humanRuling).
reviewerReport.sourceLanguageNote: Source is transliterated Akkadian (Lambert & Millard 1969). Re-parsed independently per Hard Rule 1; cited against CAD (Chicago Assyrian Dictionary) and AHw (von Soden) where lines diverge from a plain rendering. The prior 'reviewer-approved' status was independently re-verified, not rubber-stamped.

glossaryReview.reasoning: Individual glosses (siru/damu/tiddu) are direct; reading the three as a unified anthropogonic triad is the standard scholarly synthesis. claim_type 'inferred' is the honest, correct label — a reasonable reading, not a bare lexical fact.

The lexical glosses (rigmu 'noise', huburu 'clamor') are direct; the overpopulation-control interpretation is a named-scholar reading (Kilmer, Moran). claim_type 'inferred' is correct; the reading is foundational Assyriology and defensible.

reviewerReport.glossaryClaimTypeAudit: Book glossary: 20 direct, 2 inferred, 0 speculative. segments.label: The frame — the gods bear the labor (Lambert–Millard I:1–6)

i18n.en: When the gods, like man,

notes.official: *inūma ilū awīlum* is the celebrated title-line. *awīlum* is syntactically disputed: Lambert–Millard (1969) and von Soden read it as a comparative — 'When the gods, **like** man, bore the labor' — the gods themselves doing man's work before humankind existed; Foster (2005) renders the identity 'When the gods **were** man.' The translation keeps the Lambert–Millard comparative as the critical-edition baseline. The sense is stable either way: before humans, the gods bore their own toil. The identity reading is the more lens-congenial one; it is documented, not adopted — see the frame-crux glossary entry.

i18n.en: bore the labor and carried the toil-basket —

notes.official: *dullu* 'toil, corvée-labor' and *šupšikku* 'earth-carrying / labor-basket' are the poem's thesis-vocabulary: the whole narrative exists to explain why humankind bears the *dullu* of the gods. *dullu* is governed by the central entry `du-lum-dullu-divine-toil-relieved-by-humans-cross-corpus`; Atra-ḫasīs is the principal Akkadian locus for its Akkadian-side activation (deferred at Adapa, where the keyword did not survive).

i18n.en: the labor-basket of the gods was great,
the labor was heavy, the distress was much.
The great Anunnaku, the Seven,
were making the Igigi bear the labor.

segments.label: The great gods divide the cosmos (Lambert–Millard I:7–16)

i18n.en: Their father Anu was king;
their counsellor, the warrior Enlil;
their throne-bearer was Ninurta;
and their sheriff was Ennugi.
The gods clasped hands and cast the lot,
the great gods made the division:
Anu went up to the heavens,
[Enlil took] the earth for his people;
the bolt, the bar of the sea,
they gave to Enki the prince.

segments.label: The Igigi dig the Tigris, the Euphrates, and the Apsû (Lambert–Millard I:21–33, selective)

preceding_lacuna.text: Intervening lines I:17–20 (the descent of Enki to the Apsû, transition to the Igigi's toil) are not reconstructed in this draft.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: lines I:17–20 are not reconstructed in this draft, which curates the labor-frame and the creation core.]
They dug out the Tigris river,
and the Euphrates thereafter.
In the depths they opened the springs,
they set in place the Apsû.

segments.label: The years of toil and the night rebellion (Lambert–Millard I:37–71, selective)

preceding_lacuna.text: Intervening lines I:26–36 (the counting of the years of toil) are compressed; the draft resumes at the tally of years and the grumbling.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: lines I:26–36 are compressed in this draft.]
For [ … ] years they bore the labor;

notes.official: The number of years of toil is damaged. It has been read as '40 years' and as '3600 (*šār*) years'; the surviving traces do not settle it (Lambert–Millard 1969). The translation leaves it open ('[ … ] years'). The 3600-reading is the sexagesimal great-cycle (*šār*) and would resonate with the long antediluvian spans of the Sumerian King List; the 40-reading is a conventional round span. A textual, not a lexical, crux.

i18n.en: night and day.
They were grumbling in the excavation-pit,
all of them together kept up a complaint.
"Every one of us gods has declared war!"
They set fire to their tools,
they burnt their spades in the fire,
and their labor-baskets they burnt in the fire.
In the night they marched,
they surrounded the gate of Enlil's house.

segments.label: The council of Anu, Enlil, and Enki (Lambert–Millard I:72–170, selective)

preceding_lacuna.text: The council scene (Nusku rousing Enlil, Enlil's fright and tears, the summoning of Anu and Enki, the deadlock over the ringleader) is reconstructed only in outline here; many lines I:72–169 are not reproduced in this draft.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: the council dialogue I:72–169 is given only in outline in this draft.]
Nusku roused Enlil his lord,
Enlil — his tears were flowing.
Anu came down from the heavens,
and Enki [came up] from the Apsû.
"Who is the instigator of the battle?"
The gods, all of them, had decreed the corvée.

segments.label: Enki's plan — the creation of the lullû to bear the labor (Lambert–Millard I:189–199)

preceding_lacuna.text: Lines I:170–188 (the transition from the deadlock to Enki's address) are not reconstructed in this draft; the creation core resumes at Enki's proposal.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: lines I:170–188 are not reconstructed in this draft.]
Enki opened his mouth
and addressed the great gods:
"While Bēlet-ilī, the womb-goddess, is present,
let the womb-goddess create a lullû,

notes.official: *lullû* (retained, glossed 'primeval human') is the anthropogonic keyword: the first human as a fashioned creature. Lambert–Millard render 'man'; CAD L 242 gives 'primitive/savage man'; Foster 'a mortal.' The term is preserved untranslated because none of these is consensus and the reader should see the technical word (cf. Enūma Eliš VI:6 *lullâ lū amēlu*). Cross-corpus to Sumerian *lu2-u18-lu* and thematically to Hebrew *ʾādām*.

i18n.en: and let him be the bearer of the yoke.
Let him carry the yoke, the task imposed by Enlil,
let man bear the labor of the gods."

notes.official: *awīlum lišši dulli ilī* 'let man bear the toil of the gods' is the thesis-line of Mesopotamian anthropogony (Lambert–Millard 1969; Kilmer 1972): humankind is fashioned expressly to carry the *dullu* the gods no longer wish to bear. This purpose-of-creation stands in pointed contrast to Genesis 1:26–27, where humankind is made in the divine *ṣelem/dĕmût* ('image/likeness') to rule — a 'labor-vs-image' contrast that comparative scholarship (Clifford 1994; Middleton 2005) reads as two divergent valuations of the human. The line is rendered plainly; the reading is in the Akkadian and needs no gloss.

i18n.en: They summoned and questioned the goddess,
the womb-goddess, wise Bēlet-ilī:
"You are the womb-goddess, creatress of mankind;
create the lullû, that he may bear the yoke!"

segments.label: The slaughter of Wê-ila and the mixing of flesh, blood, and clay (Lambert–Millard I:200–229)

i18n.en: Nintu opened her mouth
and addressed the great gods:
"It is not proper for me to make him;
the task belongs to Enki.
He it is who purifies everything;
let him give me the clay, and I will do it."
Enki opened his mouth
and addressed the great gods:

lines.translit: i-na wa-ar-ḫi-im u4-1-kam u4-7-kam ù u4-15-kam

i18n.en: "On the first, the seventh, and the fifteenth of the month
I will make a purification, a cleansing-bath.
Let one god be slaughtered,
that the gods may be cleansed by his slaughter.
With the flesh of the god and (his) blood

notes.official: The creation-substances appear as a triad: *šīru* 'flesh' + *damu* 'blood' of the slain god, kneaded into *ṭiṭṭu* 'clay' (I:212–215, 224–225). The individual glosses are uncontested; the triad as a unit is the defining Mesopotamian anthropogony — clay animated by a god's flesh and blood (Kilmer 1972; Moran 1970; Batto 1992). Comparative note: Genesis 2:7 shares the clay/dust (*ʿāfār*, *ḥōmer*) but has **no** slain deity and **no** blood — the human is dust animated by *nišmat ḥayyîm* 'the breath of life.' The parallel is in the clay and the animation; the divergence is the theomachic blood. Flagged as a central-glossary triad candidate (Akkadian *šīru/damu/ṭiṭṭu* ↔ Hebrew *bāśār/dām/ʿāfār–ḥōmer*).

i18n.en: let Nintu mix the clay,
so that god and man
may be mixed together in the clay.

lines.translit: a-na du-úr da-ar up-pa i ni-iš-me
lines.cuneiform: 𒀀𒈾 𒁺 𒁕𒅈 𒌒𒉺 𒄿 𒉌𒅖𒈨

i18n.en: For all time let us hear the drum(?),

notes.official: *uppu* is a classic crux: 'drum' (Lambert–Millard 1969); the heartbeat/pulse; or a token of the ghost's presence. Abusch (1998) ties *uppu* to the *eṭemmu* and the *ittu* 'sign' of the next line — the throb the living 'hear for all time' is the drum-beat of the indwelling ghost. 'Drum(?)' is retained, marked uncertain; not adjudicated.

i18n.en: from the flesh of the god let there be a spirit (eṭemmu);

notes.official: *eṭemmu* (retained, glossed 'spirit'; Lambert–Millard 'ghost') is the enduring divine element left in humankind from the slain god's flesh. In Akkadian belief the *eṭemmu* is specifically the ancestral ghost sustained by *kispu* offerings (CAD E 397), not a generic soul. The human being is thus part-clay, part-divine, and the divine part is the *eṭemmu*.

i18n.en: let it make the living know its sign,
so that he not be forgotten, let the spirit remain.
"Yes!" they answered in their assembly,
the great Anunna who decree the fates.

lines.translit: il-qú-ú-ma we-e i-la ša i-šu-ú ṭe4-e-ma
lines.cuneiform: 𒅋𒈠 𒉿𒂊 𒄿𒆷 𒊭 𒄿𒋗 𒋼𒂊𒈠

i18n.en: They took Wê-ila, who had ṭēmu (intelligence),

notes.official: This line carries the double pun that is the etymological heart of the anthropogony (Lambert–Millard 1969; Moran 1970; Abusch 1998). The slaughtered god **Wê-ila** (OB *we-e i-la*; also read Wê-e, Aw-ila, Ilawēla) 'who had **ṭēmu**' (intelligence/reason) yields, by wordplay, both *awīlu* 'man' (**Wê + ila**) and *eṭemmu* 'ghost' (**ṭēmu → eṭemmu**). Humankind's very being and its indwelling spirit are both etymologically derived from the slain god. *ṭēmu* is rendered 'intelligence' plainly; the god's reason passes into humanity — that, and no engineered-cognition reading, is what the text states.

i18n.en: and slaughtered him in their assembly.
From his flesh and his blood
Nintu mixed the clay.
For all time they heard the drum(?).
From the flesh of the god a spirit (eṭemmu) came into being.
It made the living know its sign;
so that he not be forgotten, the spirit remained.

segments.label: The Igigi spit on the clay; Mami's speech (Lambert–Millard I:230–248)

i18n.en: After she had mixed that clay,
she summoned the Anunna, the great gods.
The Igigi, the great gods,
spat upon the clay.

notes.official: *ruʾtu* 'spittle': the Igigi 'spat upon the clay.' The rendering is standard and uncontested; the act's function is interpretively open — animation, ritual ratification/assent, or the contribution of a further divine bodily-substance so that ALL the Igigi (not only the one slain god) add themselves to humankind. The plain rendering is kept; the options are noted here, not imported into the text.

i18n.en: Mami opened her mouth
and addressed the great gods:
"The task you commanded me,
I have completed it.
You have slaughtered a god together with his ṭēmu (intelligence).
I have removed your heavy labor,
I have imposed your labor-basket upon man.
You have bestowed clamor upon mankind;
I have loosed the yoke, I have established freedom(?).

notes.official: *urûtam* is disputed: 'freedom/release' (giving the loosed-yoke // established-freedom parallelism, Lambert–Millard 1969) or 'the birth-stool' (the *urû* of childbirth, AHw 1435, fitting the birth-goddess context). 'Freedom(?)' is retained on the parallelism argument, marked uncertain; the birth-stool reading is noted. Verification pending.

segments.label: The fourteen pieces of clay — seven male, seven female (Lambert–Millard I:249–276, selective)

i18n.en: They heard this speech of hers,
the gods kissed her feet, (saying):
"Formerly we would call you Mami,

lines.translit: i-na-an-na be-le-et ka-la i-li lu šu-um-ki
lines.cuneiform: 𒄿𒈾𒀭𒈾 𒁁𒇷𒀉 𒅗𒆷 𒄿𒇷 𒇻 𒋗𒌝𒆠

i18n.en: now let your name be Mistress-of-all-the-gods."
They entered the house of destiny,
Enki and the wise womb-goddess.
The womb-goddesses were assembled,
and in her presence he trod the clay.
She kept reciting the incantation,
Enki, seated before her, prompted her.
When she had finished her incantation,
she nipped off fourteen pieces of clay:

notes.official: The birth-goddess nips off fourteen pieces of clay — seven set on the right (*imittu*, the male portions), seven on the left (*šumēlu*, the female), a birth-brick (*libittu*) between them (I:261–263) — and the womb-goddesses fashion seven male and seven female: the first human pairs, made to carry the yoke of the gods. The seven-and-seven pattern is the Mesopotamian primal-humanity numeral.

i18n.en: seven pieces she set on the right,
seven pieces on the left.
Between them she placed a brick.
The womb-goddesses were gathered,
seven and seven they fashioned: seven male,
seven female they fashioned.
The womb-goddess, creatress of destiny,
two by two she completed them,
the forms of the people Mami designed.
